title: Friuli-Venezia Giulia
description: Between the Alps and the Adriatic: precise whites and the modern home of orange wine.
L: Friuli-Venezia Giulia is Italy's north-eastern corner, bordered by Austria to the north and Slovenia to the east, with the Adriatic to the south. The best vineyards are in the eastern hills: Collio and Colli Orientali del Friuli, on the Slovenian border. The flat Grave plain, in the centre, makes larger volumes.

The climate is shaped by both the Alps, which protect from cold northern winds, and the Adriatic, which brings warm, humid air. The meeting creates a good day and night range and plenty of rain. The hills' soil, ponca, a layered marl and sandstone, drains well and gives mineral, structured whites.
A layered marl and sandstone soil
Ponca gives Friuli's hill whites their structure.

Friuli has been Roman, Venetian, Austrian and Italian, and its eastern hills continue into Slovenia's Brda. Collio and Brda share grapes, soils and traditions, divided by a border drawn after the Second World War. That crossroads culture shows in its food and in its openness to new and old winemaking.
Friuli's Collio continues across the border into Slovenia.
Yes, as Brda, with similar soils and grapes.
Friuli is Italy's north-eastern corner, near Slovenia
The Alps and Adriatic shape its climate
Ponca soils give its hill whites structure

About 80% of Friuli's wine is white. Friulano, formerly Tocai Friulano, gives full, almond-scented whites; it was renamed in 2008 after the EU protected Hungary's Tokaji name. Ribolla Gialla gives crisp, citrus whites and is key to orange wines. Pinot Grigio, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay are widely grown.

Reds include Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso, dark and tart; Schioppettino, peppery and fragrant; and Pignolo, tannic. Merlot and Cabernet Franc are also grown. Picolit, a sweet white, made from dried grapes, was once famous at European courts; Ramandolo is another sweet white, from Verduzzo.
Match each grape to its style.
Friuli grows native and international grapes.
Friulano was called Tocai until 2008. Old bottles and older Italian drinkers may still use the name.
The EU protected Hungary's Tokaji name

Explain how orange wine is made
Explain Friuli's role in its revival

Orange, or amber, wine is made from white grapes fermented on their skins, like a red, for days, weeks or months. Skins give the wine an amber colour, tannin, texture and flavours of dried fruit, tea, nuts and orange peel. It's an ancient method, preserved in Georgia, with its clay qvevri.

In the late 1990s, Friuli producers like Josko Gravner and Stanko Radikon, in Oslavia in the Collio, began making long skin-contact whites, mainly from Ribolla Gialla. Gravner travelled to Georgia and from 2001 fermented in buried qvevri. Their wines inspired a worldwide orange wine movement.
Which grape is central to Friuli's orange wines?
Ribolla Gialla's thick skins suit long maceration.

Orange wines are dry, with tannin and texture unusual for white wine, and flavours of apricot, orange peel, tea, honey and nuts. Many are made with minimal intervention, little or no sulphur, and natural yeasts. They're often served slightly warmer than whites, around 12 to 14 degrees, in larger glasses.
What do skins give an orange wine?
Orange wines are dry; skins don't add sugar.
Orange wine ferments white grapes on their skins
Gravner and Radikon in Friuli revived it from the late 1990s
It's dry, tannic and textured, served a little warmer
Reading Friuli and eating with it

Friuli labels usually name the grape and the DOC, like Collio Friulano or Friuli Colli Orientali Ribolla Gialla. Ramandolo and Colli Orientali del Friuli Picolit are DOCGs for sweet wines. Rosazzo is a small DOCG for white blends. Orange wines may say macerato or skin contact, or be labelled as table wine.

Friulano is traditionally paired with prosciutto di San Daniele, Friuli's famous ham. Crisp whites suit seafood from the Adriatic; orange wines suit richer dishes, mushrooms, pork, aged cheese and spiced food. Refosco suits game and sausages; Picolit suits blue cheese and pastries.
Which ham is a classic match for Friulano?
San Daniele is Friuli's own ham.
Orange wines' tannin and texture suit food that would overwhelm most whites, like roast pork or mushroom risotto.
Orange wines are usually served ice cold.
Not true. They're often served at 12 to 14 degrees, slightly warmer than most whites.
